channel.title: Juan W. Hong, Attorney at Law — Korean Law Guides for Foreign Nationals
channel.description: Plain-English guides to Korean law for foreign residents — immigration and visas, criminal defense, employment, real estate, family law, and tax.

item.title: Threats in Korea (협박죄): Penalty, Texts and Dropping the Case
item.description: Threatening someone is 협박 in Korea: up to 3 years or 5M won (Criminal Act Art. 283), but no prosecution against the victim's wish. Not with a weapon.

item.title: Falsely Accused in Korea? False Accusation (무고죄) Explained
item.description: Filing a knowingly false report to get someone punished is 무고 in Korea: up to 10 years or 15M won (Criminal Act Art. 156). What to do if you're falsely accused.

item.title: Embezzlement in Korea (횡령): Penalties and How to Respond
item.description: Accused of embezzlement (횡령) in Korea? Up to 5 years, or 10 if it happened at work (Criminal Act Arts. 355-356). What counts and how to respond.

item.title: Collect a Debt in Korea Without a Hearing: Payment Order (지급명령)
item.description: Owed money in Korea? A payment order (지급명령) has no hearing: if the debtor does not object within 2 weeks of service, it works like a final judgment.

item.title: Trade Dispute With a Korean Company: Arbitration or Court?
item.description: Unpaid invoice or defective shipment from a Korean partner? A Korean attorney explains KCAB arbitration vs Korean courts, the CISG and freezing assets.

item.title: Re-entry Permit in Korea: Leaving Without Losing Your Visa
item.description: Leaving Korea for months? Most registered foreigners need no re-entry permit for 1 year (F-5: 2 years), but never past their stay. A Korean attorney explains.

item.title: Electric Scooter Laws in Korea: Licence, Helmet and Fines
item.description: Riding a rental e-scooter (전동킥보드) in Korea needs a licence that covers mopeds. A Korean attorney explains the helmet, sidewalk, drinking and accident rules.

item.title: Obstruction of Business (업무방해) in Korea: Bar and Shop Disputes
item.description: A scene in a Korean bar or shop can be a minor offence or obstruction of business (업무방해), up to 5 years. A Korean attorney explains the line and your visa.

item.title: Hit a Taxi Driver in Korea? Why It Is Not Simple Assault
item.description: A shove in a taxi can be charged as assaulting a driver, an aggravated crime in Korea. A Korean attorney explains the penalties, settlement and your visa.

item.title: Employer Keeping Your Passport in Korea? It Is Illegal
item.description: Your employer in Korea keeps your passport or residence card "for safekeeping"? A Korean attorney explains why it is unlawful and how to get it back.

item.title: Gym or Pilates Refund in Korea: Cancel a Membership Early
item.description: Months left on a gym or pilates membership in Korea? A Korean attorney explains your right to cancel any time, the refund formula and what to do if refused.

item.title: Commercial Lease in Korea: Renewal, Rent Caps and Key Money
item.description: Opening a café, shop or office in Korea? A Korean attorney explains the commercial lease law: 10-year renewal, the 5% rent cap, key money and eviction.

item.title: Divorced Abroad, Still Married in Korea? Recording the Divorce
item.description: A divorce granted abroad does not update the Korean family register by itself. A Korean attorney explains recognition, the filing, and what still needs a court.

item.title: Scammed on a Secondhand App in Korea? What to Do Next
item.description: Paid for an item that never came? A Korean attorney explains what to do after a secondhand-trade scam in Korea: evidence, police report and getting money back.

item.title: Korean vs English Employment Contract: Which One Counts
item.description: Foreign employees in Korea often sign two versions of one contract. A Korean attorney explains which language governs and what to check before signing.

item.title: E-2 Visa Medical Check in Korea: Drug Test and Timing
item.description: A drug screen sits inside the routine E-2 medical check (채용신체검사). A Korean attorney explains what is tested, the timing and what a positive result means.

item.title: KIIP in Korea: What It Is Worth and Who Should Bother
item.description: KIIP (사회통합프로그램) shortens several immigration paths in Korea. A Korean attorney explains the levels, what completion replaces and who should actually bother.

item.title: Can Foreign Workers Join a Union in Korea?
item.description: Union rights in Korea attach to workers, not to visa status. A Korean attorney explains who may join, unfair labour practice and protection from retaliation.

item.title: Minimum Wage in Korea: What Foreign Workers Are Actually Owed
item.description: Korea's minimum wage applies to foreign workers on the same terms. A Korean attorney explains weekly holiday pay (주휴수당) and what may lawfully be deducted.

item.title: Working Outside Your Visa Category in Korea
item.description: A second job outside what your visa permits needs prior permission in Korea. A Korean attorney explains 체류자격외 활동허가 and the exposure for the employer.

item.title: Mandatory Child Abuse Reporting for Foreign Teachers in Korea
item.description: Foreign teachers and hagwon staff in Korea are mandatory reporters. A Korean attorney explains the duty, the fine for ignoring it, and good-faith protection.

item.title: Maternity and Parental Leave in Korea: Foreign Workers Qualify Too
item.description: Same rules as Korean staff: maternity leave (출산전후휴가), spousal leave and parental leave (육아휴직), paid through Employment Insurance. Who qualifies, how to ask.

item.title: Called In as a Witness in Korea
item.description: Korean police may call you in 'just as a reference'. A Korean attorney explains how a 참고인 becomes a 피의자 and what you may refuse to answer before going.

item.title: When Your Korean Employer Shuts Down or Stops Paying
item.description: Wages stop, the office empties, and your visa is tied to the company. A Korean attorney explains the wage guarantee fund and the immigration clock that starts.

item.title: Borrowed-Name Accounts in Korea: The Risk of Lending Your Name
item.description: A borrowed-name (차명) bank account, business or phone line in Korea: lending your name is often the offence itself. A Korean attorney explains the liability.

item.title: Buying a Used Car in Korea as a Foreigner
item.description: The inspection report is a legal document, and most disputes turn on it. A Korean attorney explains dealer versus private sale, the warranty and the transfer.

item.title: Someone Died in Korea? Death Report, Repatriation, 3-Month Rule
item.description: A family member died in Korea: get several death certificates, file the death report, arrange repatriation or cremation, and decide on the debts in 3 months.

item.title: Resigning From a Job in Korea: Notice Period and Final Pay
item.description: No Korean employer can compel you to keep working, but how you resign decides your final pay, benefits and visa. A Korean attorney explains the notice rules.

item.title: Theft and Shoplifting Charges in Korea for Foreigners
item.description: Korean theft law (절도) has no minimum value, and repaying the shop does not end it. A Korean attorney explains detention risk and suspended indictment.

item.title: Extortion in Korean: 공갈 (Gonggal) and When a Demand Is a Crime
item.description: Extortion in Korean is 공갈 (gonggal). Where a lawful settlement (합의) demand ends and extortion begins, and why paying quietly is rarely the safe option.

item.title: Brokerage Commission and Maintenance Fees in Korea
item.description: The rent is not the whole rent. A Korean attorney explains how brokerage commission (중개보수) is capped and what a maintenance fee (관리비) may lawfully contain.

item.title: 기소유예 in English: Suspended Indictment vs 선고유예 vs 집행유예
item.description: 기소유예 in English is a suspended indictment: the prosecutor files no charge. 선고유예 = sentence withheld; 집행유예 = prison suspended. What each means for your visa.

item.title: Changing Your Visa Status Inside Korea
item.description: A status change permit (체류자격 변경허가) is not an extension. A Korean attorney explains which switches need you to leave Korea and when late filing means overstay.

item.title: Hit-and-Run in Korea: Leaving Without Your Details Is Fleeing
item.description: In Korea, injury plus driving off is 도주치상 under the Aggravated Punishment Act, and insurance does not cure it. What counts as fleeing, and what to do now.

item.title: Enrolling a Foreign Child in a Korean Public School
item.description: Korean public schools admit foreign children on proof of residence, not visa status. A Korean attorney explains enrollment (취학) and what if a school refuses.

item.title: Damages Without a Second Lawsuit: The Compensation Order
item.description: A crime victim in Korea need not sue twice. A Korean attorney explains the compensation order (배상명령): which offences qualify and what it can actually cover.

item.title: Seven Days: Appealing a Criminal Conviction in Korea
item.description: An appeal (항소) in Korea runs on a seven-day clock that starts at pronouncement. A Korean attorney explains the grounds deadline and what the court reviews.

item.title: Power of Attorney in Korea From Abroad: Apostille or Consulate
item.description: Signing a 위임장 outside Korea: notarise and apostille, or sign at the Korean consulate. Why banks refuse broad wording, and what the document must name.

item.title: D-8 Corporate Investment Visa in Korea: How It Works
item.description: The money does not buy a D-8 visa (기업투자) — the foreign-investment report does. A Korean attorney explains the order of steps, the minimum and subcategories.

item.title: Immigration Detention in Korea: Temporary Release
item.description: Immigration detention (보호) in Korea is administrative, not criminal. A Korean attorney explains temporary release (보호일시해제) and the routes out that matter.

item.title: Non-Compete and Confidentiality Clauses in Korea
item.description: A Korean non-compete (경업금지) is neither void nor automatically valid. A Korean attorney explains the six factors and the injunction that lands before trial.

item.title: Criminal Trial in Korea as a Foreigner: The Courtroom Sequence
item.description: Interpretation covers the hearing, not the case file. A Korean attorney explains the order a Korean criminal trial (공판) follows and the seven days after it.

item.title: Winning Is Not Collecting: Enforcing a Judgment in Korea
item.description: A Korean judgment does not move money on its own. A Korean attorney explains enforcement titles, property disclosure and the three routes of execution (강제집행).

item.title: Working Hours, Overtime and Annual Leave in Korea
item.description: Korean working time turns on two numbers. A Korean attorney explains the 52-hour ceiling, the premiums, the under-five exemption and annual leave (연차).

item.title: Your Record on Paper: Criminal Record Certificates in Korea
item.description: Korea keeps convictions and investigations on two separate records. A Korean attorney explains which certificate shows what and how long entries stay there.

item.title: Settling a Criminal Case in Korea: The Victim Agreement
item.description: A settlement (합의) ends some Korean prosecutions outright and only reduces others. A Korean attorney explains which offences, and what the paper must say.

item.title: Turned Back at the Border: Entry Refusal at a Korean Airport
item.description: A Korean visa is permission to travel, not a right to be admitted. A Korean attorney explains entry refusal (입국불허), secondary inspection and what you sign.

item.title: Appealing a Korean Immigration Decision: When the Answer Is No
item.description: Refused an extension or served a departure order? A Korean attorney explains the three appeal routes, the 90-day clock, and why filing does not stop removal.

item.title: Limitation Periods in Korea: The Deadlines That Decide a Case
item.description: Korean law puts a deadline on nearly every claim, running from earlier than you think. A Korean attorney explains the civil, criminal and labour periods (시효).

item.title: After the Marriage Ends: Keeping an F-6 Visa in Korea
item.description: Divorce does not automatically end an F-6 visa, but keeping it means proving the Korean spouse's fault (귀책사유). A Korean attorney explains the F-6-3 route.

item.title: Fixed-Term Contract in Korea (기간제): the 2-Year Rule Explained
item.description: In Korea, fixed-term contracts that add up to more than 2 years become open-ended employment (무기계약직), and some non-renewals count as dismissal. Exceptions and visa.

item.title: Illegal Filming Charges in Korea: Phone Forensics and Penalties
item.description: Illegal filming (불법촬영) in Korea carries up to seven years, and watching the footage is a separate offence. A Korean attorney explains the phone forensics.

item.title: Freezing the Money First: Provisional Attachment in Korea
item.description: Winning against an empty account is worth nothing. A Korean attorney explains provisional attachment (가압류): what can be frozen, the cost and the counter-move.

item.title: The D-4 Language Student Visa in Korea
item.description: A D-4 visa (어학연수) buys a language course, not a life in Korea. A Korean attorney explains attendance, the part-time work permit and the route to a D-2.

item.title: Departure Ban in Korea: Why You Can't Leave and How to Lift It
item.description: Under investigation in Korea? The measure is a departure suspension (출국정지), usually found at check-in. A Korean attorney explains the two ways to fight it.

item.title: Court Papers in Korean: What to Do When You Are Sued in Korea
item.description: A payment order gives you two weeks, a complaint thirty days, and silence lets the court decide without you. A Korean attorney explains each envelope.

item.title: Accused of Indecent Act by Force in Korea
item.description: Indecent act by force (강제추행) is charged broadly in Korea and settlement no longer ends it. A Korean attorney explains registration and immigration fallout.

item.title: Applying for Refugee Status in Korea
item.description: Refugee status (난민) in Korea turns on an interview and appeals measured in days. A Korean attorney explains the routes and how humanitarian stay differs.

item.title: Sending Money Out of Korea: Why Transfers Get Blocked
item.description: Korean banks block outbound transfers over documents, not amounts. A Korean attorney explains the foreign exchange rules (외국환거래) and split remittances.

item.title: Alien Registration and Address Reporting in Korea
item.description: Alien registration and the 14-day change-of-address report are easy to forget and costly. A Korean attorney explains the deadlines, fines and renewal risk.
